references.text: The two disciples on the way to Emmaus now recounted what had happened "on the road" – precisely that road described in [ref:Luk 24:13-16|Luke 24:13-16], where Jesus joined them without their recognizing him.

The disciples told how Jesus was recognized "when he broke bread" – this points directly back to [ref:Luk 24:30-31|Luke 24:30-31], where Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened.

The breaking of bread at Emmaus has a clear connection to the institution of the Lord's Supper in [ref:Luk 22:19|Luke 22:19], where Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to the disciples – the same sequence of actions as at the meal in Emmaus.
The breaking of bread as a sign of recognition in Emmaus points forward to the early church's practice of breaking bread together, as described in [ref:Apg 2:42|Acts 2:42].
The continued practice of breaking bread in homes in [ref:Apg 2:46|Acts 2:46] reflects the meal at Emmaus where Jesus was recognized in the breaking of bread.

What the disciples reported about "what had happened on the road" includes Jesus' explanation of the Scriptures as described in [ref:Luk 24:25-27|Luke 24:25-27], where he opened the Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and all the prophets.

In [ref:Mark 16:12-13|Mark 16:12-13] there is a parallel to the Emmaus account, where Jesus appeared in another form to two of the disciples who were walking, and they went back and told it to the others.

Paul links the breaking of bread to fellowship with Christ in [ref:1 Kor 10:16|1 Corinthians 10:16], where the cup of blessing and the bread we break are a sharing in the body of Christ – a theological elaboration on recognition through the breaking of bread.
